reason: The text (Genesis 4) presents two brothers of equal standing from the same parents. Their divergent fates—Abel's offering being accepted and Cain's being rejected—are determined by their righteousness and the quality of their actions, not by inherent elite status. The Lord explicitly tells Cain that acceptance depends on doing well (proper conduct), not on any innate superiority or inferiority. When Cain sins by murdering Abel, he is cursed despite any social position. The narrative structure emphasizes that moral agency and righteous action matter more than social class or elite status, and that even those in humble occupations (shepherds, farmers) stand equal before divine judgment.
